content.intro: In this lesson, you will study exception handling best practices with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you report and recover from expected failures while ensuring resources are released. In this lesson, focus on avoiding empty catch blocks and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Concurrency introduces shared-state ordering and cancellation concerns. Prefer task abstractions and immutable data where possible, coordinate access explicitly, and always define shutdown, timeout, and failure behavior. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect avoiding empty catch blocks with avoiding exceptions for routine control flow before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Avoiding empty catch blocks
items.text: Concurrency introduces shared-state ordering and cancellation concerns. Prefer task abstractions and immutable data where possible, coordinate access explicitly, and always define shutdown, timeout, and failure behavior.

items.title: Avoiding exceptions for routine control flow
items.text: Exceptions report conditions that interrupt the normal path. Catch only when the code can recover or add context, preserve the original cause, and use try-with-resources for closeable resources.

items.title: Preserving useful stack traces
items.text: Measure before tuning. Use JVM diagnostics and representative workloads to distinguish allocation pressure, retained objects, CPU work, blocking, and thread contention.

items.title: Handling errors at the appropriate layer
items.text: Exceptions describe abnormal or rejected operations. Catch an exception only when you can recover or add useful context, preserve causes, and prefer try-with-resources for closeable resources. Apply that reasoning specifically to handling errors at the appropriate layer and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Avoiding disclosure of internal details in user-facing messages
items.text: Primitive variables store values of the eight primitive types. Choose a type that represents the domain and range required; use exact decimal arithmetic for monetary values when appropriate.

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

common_mistakes.problem: Applying the rule from memory without checking its exact contract.
common_mistakes.why: Small differences in type, scope, API version, or input shape can change the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the relevant official API/language documentation and build a minimal reproducer.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.
